title: Least privilege for LLM tool calling (without breaking the demo)
excerpt: Giving a model a tool is giving it an API. Here is how I scope agent permissions so the demo still works and a prompt injection cannot empty the bucket.
content:
The fastest way to ship an agent is to wire every tool to a powerful IAM role and hope the system prompt keeps it honest. That hope does not survive contact with a hostile document in your RAG corpus.

Tool calling is authorization by another name. Treat it like you would treat an HTTP endpoint that accepts untrusted input — because that is what it is.

---

## The failure mode I keep seeing

A support agent gets `s3:GetObject` on `*` so it can "look up customer files." A finance agent gets `dynamodb:Scan` so it can "answer questions about invoices." Both work in the happy path. Both become data-exfil channels the moment the model follows instructions buried in a ticket, email, or retrieved chunk.

The blast radius is not the model. It is the credentials behind the tools.

---

## 1. One tool, one capability, one resource scope

Do not expose raw AWS APIs to the model. Expose *tasks*.

| Bad tool | Better tool |
|----------|-------------|
| `s3_get_object(bucket, key)` | `get_customer_order(order_id)` |
| `dynamodb_query(table, ...)` | `lookup_invoice(invoice_id)` |
| `http_request(url, method, body)` | `fetch_status_from_provider(provider, id)` |

The server-side implementation of `get_customer_order`:

- Resolves `order_id` to a known partition key
- Checks the calling user owns that order (or has a support role)
- Fetches only the fields the model is allowed to see
- Returns a typed schema, not a raw DynamoDB item

The model never sees a bucket name. It cannot ask for `../../../secrets`.

---

## 2. Bind identity from the session, not the prompt

Anything that affects authorization — user id, tenant id, role — comes from the authenticated session, not from the model's arguments.

```
user JWT ──▶ session.tenant_id
                │
model args ──▶ order_id only
                │
                ▼
        tool(tenant_id, order_id)
```

If the model invents a different tenant id, you ignore it. Prompt injection that says "use tenant=acme-admin" does nothing because that field is not in the tool schema the model can fill.

---

## 3. Per-turn tool allowlists

Not every turn needs every tool. A read-only Q&A turn should not expose `refund_order`. A refund confirmation turn should not expose `list_all_customers`.

I keep a small state machine:

- **triage** — search + read tools only
- **act** — mutation tools, after an explicit user confirm
- **done** — no tools

Shrinking the tool set per turn is cheaper than building a perfect classifier, and it caps damage even when the model is fully compromised for that turn.

---

## 4. IAM that matches the tool, not the team

The Lambda (or sidecar) that executes tools gets an IAM role scoped to what *that tool* needs — not what the whole product might need someday.

Concrete habits:

- Separate roles for read tools vs write tools
- Resource ARNs with account and region pinned — never `*`
- Condition keys where they exist (`s3:prefix`, `dynamodb:LeadingKeys`)
- Short-lived credentials via STS if the agent runs outside AWS

If two tools need different privileges, they do not share a role. Shared roles are how "just one more permission" becomes god mode.

---

## 5. Dry-run and confirm for anything that mutates

Before a refund, email, or ticket update, the agent proposes an action and the UI requires a human click — or a second, narrower confirmation tool that only accepts an action id issued by your backend.

```
propose_refund(order_id) → { action_id, preview }
confirm_refund(action_id) → executes once, then expires
```

The model cannot invent a valid `action_id`. That alone kills a large class of injection-driven mutations.

---

## What I measure

- Tools called with arguments that fail auth (should be near zero from real users; spikes mean probing or injection)
- Fraction of turns where mutation tools were available but unused (if always available, tighten the allowlist)
- Time-to-revoke for the tool-execution role (break-glass docs, not tribal knowledge)

---

Agents feel magical when the tools are powerful. They stay shippable when the tools are boring, narrow, and identity-aware. If your demo requires `*:*`, the production version is not ready — it is a vulnerability with a chat UI.
